video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-1ylj.title: Indirect Hot Water Heater Installation on a Steam Boiler (This Old House)
video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-1ylj.summary: This Old House demonstrates converting a steam boiler that serves a house with radiant heat into a domestic hot water source by installing an indirect hot water heater. The video explains the limitations of boiler-derived hot water and then details an indirect tank with an internal coil that transfers heat from boiler water to a larger volume of potable water, eliminating the need for a direct-flame water heater. The program covers the tank’s construction (stainless steel, thick insulation), coil arrangement, filtration to protect the system, and the piping and valve hardware required (temperating valve, aquastat, relay, and circulator). It also walks through the installation steps: isolating the boiler, draining the system, mounting and leveling the tank, copper piping and soldering, adding a feed strainer, wiring controls, and starting the system to verify hot water supply.

video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-25gy.title: Wet-Tap Water Main Upgrade and Copper Service Installation (Saratoga, NY) – This Old House
video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-25gy.summary: This Old House documents a street-level water and sewer upgrade at a site in Saratoga, focusing on replacing an old galvanized/lead water service and a deteriorated sewer line while avoiding disruption to a new sidewalk. The crew locates an existing water main, investigates the lead service, and plans a new drain route that begins at a manhole. They use trenching and a diamond drill approach for the sewer/drain routing, then perform a wet tap to tie into the live 4-inch water main using a Mueller B-101 tapping machine. The process includes managing high pressure with a bypass and shutoff, establishing a proper service pitch with laser-guided alignment, and tying in copper Type K service lines with curb stops to provide both domestic supply and a dedicated fire-protection line for the upper floors. The video emphasizes practical, code-conscious constraints (10-foot separation from sewer, avoiding gas lines, frostproof curb shutoffs) and highlights long-standing plumbing tools and methods still in active use (wet taps, tapping machines) within municipal systems.

video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-2ale.title: Replacing Polybutylene Piping with CPVC in a Raleigh Home
video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-2ale.summary: This Old House’s Ask This Old House episode documents a PB (polybutylene) piping replacement in a Raleigh, NC home. The segment outlines the historical prevalence of polybutylene in the 1970s, the leaks observed in PB and acetal fittings, and the decision to replace the entire PB network with CPVC hot- and cold-water lines. The crew removes the old piping through wall openings, reroutes new CPVC from the crawl space, and ties into fixtures (notably a second-floor shower valve) using brass-to-CPVC adapters and threaded/female adapters. The project requires extensive wall and ceiling access, drywall repair by a skilled tradesperson, and a final water test. The host commentary frames the replacement as both technically necessary and time-consuming, emphasizing that labor and wall restoration are major cost components alongside materials. The episode also places the work in a regional context, noting that tens of thousands of Raleigh-area homes were affected by PB piping.

video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-2ckj.title: Installing a Frost-Proof Outdoor Hydrant to Deliver Hot and Cold Water Outside (This Old House)
video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-2ckj.summary: This Old House demonstrates converting a cold outdoor garden faucet into a year-round, hot-and-cold wall hydrant that feeds exterior water with a frost-proof design. The host explains the drawbacks of a simple Y-connector approach, then installs a frost-proof wall hydrant that mounts on the exterior, with hot and cold runs brought from inside. The process covers routing copper supply from a kitchen-area crawl space, turning off the main, cutting the copper line, removing the old faucet, positioning the new hydrant (center-to-center = 5 inches), sealing the unit to vinyl with silicone, securing it with weather screws, and tying hot and cold lines together with shut-offs for future service. The final section demonstrates turning the water back on and testing the new outside faucet, which now provides hot water outdoors and eliminates winter shutoffs inside. The lesson emphasizes freeze protection and the convenience of year-round use for outdoor tasks like washing the car or pets.

video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-2l8s.summary: This Old House walkthrough explains faucet aerators, including how a built-in flow restrictor governs water through a small orifice and how debris can clog the path. The presenter demonstrates safe removal with a non-damaging wrench on an aerator with straight edges, reveals debris (notably coffee grounds) inside, flushes the spout to verify cleanliness, and decides that replacement may be more cost-effective than thorough cleaning. The segment concludes with a quick hot/cold water test to confirm restored flow and function, noting a rough replacement cost in the five to six dollar range.

video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-3akj.title: Installing a Whole-House Water Filter with Push-Fit Fittings (This Old House)
video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-3akj.summary: The video details the installation of a whole-house water filter in a garage mechanical room. It covers selecting between two cartridge types (dirt/rust and dirt/rust plus chlorine removal) to address chlorine taste, mounting the filter on a plywood-backed bracket, and modifying the plumbing with push-fit (solderless) fittings and adapters from 1 inch to 3/4 inch. The host explains shutting off water at the street curb stop, creating isolation on both sides of the filter with two shut-off valves, and grounding considerations after adding the filter. A test run follows to check for leaks, and maintenance guidance notes cartridge replacement every 2–3 months.

A torque wrench is used to snug the bands without overtightening, and the installer measures and cuts replacement pipe to fit with proper pitch. The video emphasizes careful measurement, gasket handling, and pressure-tested connections while noting a long-term (quote) “100 years” durability of the No-Hub assembly. video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-cua4.summary: This Old House walks through upgrading a retrofit snap-on faucet filtration setup to a dedicated under-sink carbon filtration system with a cartridge-indicator, highlighting the cartridge technology (carbon composite membrane), kit contents, and a step-by-step installation sequence. The workflow emphasizes proper shut-off, secure connections, and a guided diagram to minimize mis-piping, finishing with a tested, cleaner-looking installation under the sink.

video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-cwsy.title: Bottleshaped Cistern: 18th-Century Rainwater Storage in an Old House (This Old House)
video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-cwsy.summary: This Old House features historic archaeologist Suzanne Shere examining an intact, bottleshaped cistern serving as a rainwater storage system for an 18th-century house. The segment describes how the cistern was built with handmade brick, likely two bricks thick, and how bricks appear to have been reused from a chimney or fireplace. It notes the absence of a builder’s trench, mortared joints to the bottom, and a waterproof bottom surface capped with a thin paving-like layer. A large top opening suggests a trap-door for manual bucket access or a crank draw, and interior inspection reveals a depth of about seven feet and a lead pipe connected to the house basement for water delivery to a spigot. The discussion places the cistern within a broader domestic water ecosystem of the period, including wells, privies, and gardens, illustrating how early households managed water for washing, drinking, and chores within spatial constraints.

video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-cz53.title: Brooklyn, Massachusetts: Sewer Camera Inspection, Storm/Sanitary Separation, and PVC Drain Retrofit for a 1957 Addition
video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-cz53.summary: This This Old House Live segment follows Kevin and Richard as they work on a heavily renovated Brooklyn, MA home addition that connects to a municipal water and sewer system. The hosts describe the three main utilities entering the property (water supply, sanitary sewer, and storm sewer) and clarify ownership boundaries between homeowner and city, including the shut-off valve location and the responsibility line for storm drainage. The interior plan features new PVC drain lines under a slab, a future master bathroom vent and trap, and a camera inspection of the sewer line that reveals dirt buildup, a transition to orangeburg/clay pipe with root intrusion, and a sag in the town sewer. The team discusses repair options (open-cut replacement with PVC versus liner options), the cost implications of digging versus piping lining, and the need for a bonded contractor when cutting into street/sidewalk. They also cover drainage philosophy (keeping water outside the building, proper pitch and rise), and the permitting process that can impact schedule. All of this is conveyed through live Q&A and visual demonstrations using an in-camera feed on an iPad during the workflow.

video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-d4x1.title: Ice maker water line connections: saddle valves, soldered, and solderless options
video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-d4x1.summary: The video discusses how to supply an ice maker with water, focusing on saddle valves and their drawbacks, and then presenting safer, code-friendly alternatives. It explains that saddle valves clamp onto copper water lines to pierce the pipe and feed a tube to the ice maker, but notes this approach as prone to leaks, rust, and eventual failure, with legal restrictions in some jurisdictions for licensed plumbers. The speaker advocates avoiding saddle valves when possible and outlines solderless options (T-fittings with shutoff, Dutch finger clamps) and traditional soldered copper connections, along with practical tubing choices (polyethylene, other plastics, stainless steel braided, and copper) and the importance of a shutoff valve for future service. The overall guidance emphasizes safer, longer-lasting connections and the preference for copper pipe with an appropriate shutoff rather than saddle valves.

video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-dkff.title: Replacing a Kitchen Sink: Removal, Fit, and Faucet Install (Ask This Old House)
video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-dkff.summary: This Old House shows a step‑by‑step kitchen sink replacement, including turning off the water and disconnecting faucet supply lines, removing the old sink and its sealant from the countertop, adjusting a mis-sized opening with an oscillating saw, dropping in a standard replacement sink, mounting a new faucet with a base plate, applying silicone sealant, securing the sink with under-sink clips, and routing the drainage with an ABS-to-PVC adapter and a dishwasher tailpiece, followed by a final water test to confirm a leak-free install.

video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-ea5e.title: Drain Pipe Puzzle: Basement-to-Roof Drain Routing in a This Old House Renovation
video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-ea5e.summary: In this house-renovation video, the team tackles routing a full-size drainage stack through a multi-room remodel, balancing code requirements, space constraints, and existing structure. The plumber explains converting an old cast-iron stack to current practice using PVC, while coordinating with the joists, kitchen layout, and headroom to avoid clashes with the electrical panel and living spaces. The crew demonstrates removing the old cast iron with a chain cutter, installing a neoprene-gasket coupling with stainless-steel bands, and laying out a drain path that uses the joist direction for proper pitch toward the main drain and eventual roof vent. A Y-fitting creates a branch to the second-floor toilet, and the team discusses padding walls and adjusting the toilet rough-ins to accommodate the new configuration. The result emphasizes practical, code-conscious planning, precise cutting, and a clean run inside the joist bays that preserves headroom and minimizes horizontal piping.”

video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-ewsx.title: How to Shorten a Gas Pipe to Fit an Oven

video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-gkoq.title: Preventing Frozen and Burst Pipes: Outdoor Faucets, Insulation, and Heat Tape
video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-gkoq.summary: This Old House outlines practical steps to guard residential plumbing against freezing by addressing outdoor spigots, interior shut-offs, insulation, and heating options. The guidance targets homeowners and DIYers seeking preventive measures for winter-protecting domestic water lines.

video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-pe3g.title: How to Prevent Plumbing Sulfur Smells | Ask This Old House
video-plumbing-repairs-and-upgrades-pe3g.summary: This Old House explains that sulfur odors in household water typically stem from hydrogen sulfide dissolved in groundwater. The discussion covers distinguishing odor sources (hot vs cold water, well water vs municipal supply), treating well water with filtration, and a key heater-maintenance fix: the sacrificial anode rod inside tank-type water heaters. Hydrogen sulfide attacks magnesium anodes, producing the rotten-egg smell, so replacing a magnesium anode with aluminum can dramatically reduce odors. The guidance also notes municipal water is usually treated and should not carry high hydrogen sulfide levels. The video emphasizes routine maintenance (anode replacement about every two years) and consulting a local well contractor for filtration options.”
